title: Acute Diarrhoea Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute diarrhoea, recognising serious causes and dehydration risk, distinguishing infectious from inflammatory causes, and supporting safe management and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, antimicrobial guidance or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Severe dehydration (dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, weakness, hypotension, reduced urine output).
Bloody diarrhoea or signs of inflammatory bowel disease.
Severe systemic illness or sepsis (fever, shock, altered consciousness).
Toxin-mediated disease (Clostridium difficile, staphylococcal food poisoning, cholera-like).
Acute surgical abdomen (severe pain, peritonitis, obstruction).
Immunosuppression increasing infection risk or atypical presentation risk.
Medication-related (antibiotics, laxative misuse, NSAIDs).
Recent travel or unusual food exposures.
items.importantLimitation: Absence of bloody stools does not exclude serious infection or IBD. Dehydration develops rapidly especially in elderly and young children.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise diarrhoea onset, severity and associated symptoms to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Diarrhoea characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; duration (hours, days, weeks).
Frequency: number of stools per day; day and night involvement.
Consistency: watery, loose, bloody, mucoid, greasy.
Associated: abdominal pain, cramping, tenesmus, urgency.
Blood or mucus: visible blood, melena or occult blood?

items.title: Systemic and constitutional features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors or chills.
Nausea, vomiting or inability to drink.
Malaise, myalgia or headache.
Signs of dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine output, dizziness.
Recent upper-respiratory or other infection.

items.title: Risk factors and triggers
mustConfirmOrExclude: Recent antibiotic use (especially broad-spectrum; C. difficile risk).
Recent food intake or eating out (food poisoning risk).
Travel abroad or to high-risk areas.
Sick contacts or outbreak exposure.
Recent laxative or NSAID use.
Known inflammatory bowel disease.
Immunosuppression (HIV, chemotherapy, immunosuppressive drugs).

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Bloody diarrhoea or diarrhoea with mucus.
Severe abdominal pain or peritoneal signs.
High fever (>38.5Â°C) with systemic illness.
Unable to drink or persistent vomiting (dehydration risk).
Diarrhoea lasting >2 weeks (chronic diarrhoea).
Weight loss or systemic symptoms.
Recent hospitalisation or antibiotic exposure (C. difficile).

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent assessment or investigation.

items.title: Severe dehydration
urgentFeatures: Inability to drink or persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake.
Clinical signs: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, weakness.
Reduced urine output or dark urine.
Hypotension or tachycardia.
Altered consciousness or confusion.
implications: Hospital assessment for intravenous fluid replacement.

items.title: Bloody diarrhoea or inflammatory bowel disease
urgentFeatures: Visible blood or mucus in stool.
Severe abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea.
Fever with bloody diarrhoea.
History of IBD with acute exacerbation.
Tenesmus and urgency.
implications: Stool culture and testing; hospital referral if severe or high fever.

items.title: Toxic megacolon or fulminant colitis
urgentFeatures: Severe abdominal pain, distension and tenderness.
Reduced bowel sounds.
Fever, tachycardia and signs of sepsis.
Often follows Clostridium difficile or severe IBD flare.
implications: Emergency hospital assessment; abdominal imaging required.

items.title: Acute surgical abdomen
urgentFeatures: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs (rebound, guarding).
Abdominal distension or vomiting.
Fever with localised tenderness.
Signs of shock or sepsis.
implications: Emergency hospital assessment; abdominal imaging required.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine for dehydration, peritoneal signs and systemic illness.

items.title: Dehydration assessment
howToTest: Assess mucous membranes: moist, dry or very dry.
Skin turgor: normal, reduced or significantly reduced (pinch skin, measure recoil time).
Urine output: frequency and colour (dark or concentrated suggests dehydration).
Vital signs: heart rate, blood pressure (postural if possible).
normal: Moist mucous membranes, normal skin turgor, normal urine output, normal vital signs.
abnormal: Dry mucous membranes, reduced turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced/dark urine.
implications: Dehydration severity guides need for IV fluids vs. oral rehydration therapy.

items.title: Abdominal examination
howToTest: Palpate: tenderness (diffuse vs. localised), guarding, rebound, masses.
Auscultate: bowel sounds (present, reduced or absent).
abnormal: Peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound, rigid), distension, absent bowel sounds, focal tenderness.
implications: Peritoneal signs suggest serious pathology; reduced/absent bowel sounds suggest obstruction or ileus.

items.title: Systemic assessment
howToTest: Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure.
Assess general appearance: well, unwell, toxic, shocked.
Note rash (meningococcal), stigmata of liver disease or IBD (perianal tags, fistulae).
normal: Afebrile or low-grade fever, normal vital signs, well appearance.
abnormal: High fever (>38.5Â°C), tachycardia, hypotension, signs of shock or sepsis.
implications: Fever with bloody diarrhoea suggests infectious colitis; shock suggests severe infection or dehydration.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis and management decisions.

items.title: Viral gastroenteritis
commonFindings: Watery diarrhoea with or without vomiting.
Preceding viral illness or sick contact.
implications: Supportive care with oral rehydration; no antibiotics needed.

items.title: Bacterial gastroenteritis
commonFindings: Often bloody diarrhoea or diarrhoea with mucus.
Recent food intake or eating out.
implications: Stool culture if indicated; antibiotics only if severe systemic illness or specific organisms.

items.title: Clostridium difficile infection
commonFindings: Watery diarrhoea following antibiotic use (especially broad-spectrum).
Fever, abdominal pain and systemic illness.
Risk factors: recent hospitalisation, elderly, immunosuppression.
implications: Stool toxin testing; stop causative antibiotic; specific anti-C. difficile therapy if moderate/severe.

items.title: Inflammatory bowel disease exacerbation
commonFindings: Known history of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
Fever, weight loss and systemic symptoms.
implications: Specialist assessment; imaging and labs (CRP, albumin); aminosalicylates or corticosteroids.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on dehydration severity, red-flag assessment and investigation needs.

items.title: Rehydration approach
mustConfirmOrExclude: Mild dehydration: oral rehydration solution with electrolytes; small frequent amounts.
Moderate dehydration: IV fluids if unable to tolerate oral; closely monitor output.
Severe dehydration: hospital admission for IV fluids and monitoring.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: Stool culture: if bloody diarrhoea, fever or severe systemic illness.
C. difficile testing: if recent antibiotics or hospital exposure.
Blood tests: if fever >38.5Â°C or severe systemic illness (FBC, CRP, electrolytes).
Imaging: if acute surgical abdomen suspected (abdominal X-ray or CT).

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No signs of severe dehydration.
Able to tolerate oral intake.
No bloody diarrhoea or only minimal blood.
No fever or low-grade fever only.
No peritoneal signs.
Likely viral gastroenteritis or mild bacterial infection.

items.title: Hospital referral or admission
urgentFeatures: Severe dehydration with inability to drink.
Bloody diarrhoea with fever or severe systemic illness.
Peritoneal signs or suspected acute surgical abdomen.
Signs of shock or sepsis.
Severe immunosuppression (at risk for complications).
implications: Hospital assessment for fluid replacement and investigation.

items.title: Acute diarrhoea
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: signs of severe dehydration (extreme dizziness, confusion, no urine for 8+ hours); severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs; blood in stool with fever and severe systemic illness; or signs of shock.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake; bloody diarrhoea; high fever (>38.5Â°C); severe abdominal pain; diarrhoea lasting >2 weeks; or signs of dehydration (dark urine, dry mouth).
Speak to your GP if: diarrhoea persists beyond 1 week; you are not improving with rehydration; you want antibiotic advice; or you are concerned about underlying causes.
